# Record, Downmix, and Playback Loop

## Overview

This sketch demonstrates a complete audio capture and playback pipeline:
1. **Records 30 seconds** of stereo audio from dual INMP441 microphones
2. **Downmixes to mono** using HYBRID algorithm (adaptive + width)
3. **Plays back** continuously through MAX98357A speaker

## Hardware Requirements

- ESP32-S3-LCD-2 board
- 2× INMP441 MEMS microphones
- 1× MAX98357A I2S amplifier module
- 2× 1W flat mag speakers (4-8 ohm)
- Breadboard and jumper wires

## Wiring Diagram

### INMP441 Microphones → ESP32 (I2S0)

\```
ESP32-S3-LCD-2          INMP441 #1 (LEFT)      INMP441 #2 (RIGHT)
────────────────        ─────────────────      ──────────────────
3.3V ───────────┬────── VDD                    VDD
                │
GND ────────────┼────── GND ──────────┬─────── GND
                │                     │
GPIO 2 (BCK) ───┼────── SCK ──────────┼─────── SCK
GPIO 4 (WS) ────┼────── WS ───────────┼─────── WS
GPIO 18 (DIN) ──┴────── SD ───────────┴─────── SD
                        │                      │
                        L/R → GND              L/R → 3.3V
                          (LEFT)                 (RIGHT)
\```

### MAX98357A Speaker → ESP32 (I2S1)

\```
MAX98357A               ESP32-S3-LCD-2
─────────────           ────────────────
VIN    ─────────────────→ 5V (or 3.3V)
GND    ─────────────────→ GND
BCLK   ─────────────────→ GPIO 6
LRC    ─────────────────→ GPIO 7
DIN    ─────────────────→ GPIO 8
GAIN   ─────────────────→ Float (9dB) / GND (12dB) / VDD (15dB)
SD     ─────────────────→ VIN (always on)

SPK+   ─────────────────→ Speaker +
SPK-   ─────────────────→ Speaker -
\```

## Pin Summary

| Function      | ESP32 Pin | Device Pin     | Notes                          |
|---------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| **Microphones (I2S0)** |           |                |                                |
| Bit Clock     | GPIO 2    | SCK (both mics)| Shared I2S bus                 |
| Word Select   | GPIO 4    | WS (both mics) | Shared I2S bus                 |
| Data In       | GPIO 18   | SD (both mics) | Shared I2S bus                 |
| Left Channel  | —         | Mic #1 L/R → GND | Channel select                 |
| Right Channel | —         | Mic #2 L/R → 3.3V | Channel select                 |
| **Speaker (I2S1)** |           |                |                                |
| Bit Clock     | GPIO 6    | BCLK           | Camera pin (safe if no camera) |
| Word Select   | GPIO 7    | LRC            | Camera pin (safe if no camera) |
| Data Out      | GPIO 8    | DIN            | Camera pin (safe if no camera) |
| Power         | 5V        | VIN            | 3.3V also works (lower volume) |

**Important:** GPIO 6, 7, 8 are camera pins from the schematic, but safe to use when the camera is not attached.

## Audio Specifications

| Parameter       | Value              |
|-----------------|--------------------|
| Sample Rate     | 16,000 Hz          |
| Bit Depth       | 16-bit PCM         |
| Recording       | 30 seconds stereo  |
| Playback        | Mono (looped)      |
| Downmix Method  | HYBRID (adaptive + width) |
| Memory Usage    | ~1.92 MB PSRAM     |

## Downmix Algorithm: HYBRID

The HYBRID downmix algorithm combines the best of two approaches:

- **Adaptive weighting**: Favors the microphone with stronger signal (clarity)
- **30%-70% constraint**: Ensures both channels always contribute (width)

This prevents the "interruption" feeling when blocking one mic while maintaining clarity and reducing background noise compared to simple averaging.

## Usage Instructions

### 1. Wire Everything

Follow the wiring diagrams above. Critical points:

- **Microphones**: Both share I2S bus (GPIO 2, 4, 18)
  - Mic #1: L/R → **GND** (left channel)
  - Mic #2: L/R → **3.3V** (right channel)

- **Speaker**: Connect to I2S1 (GPIO 6, 7, 8)
  - Use **5V** for full power (3.3V works but quieter)
  - Connect speaker to SPK+ and SPK-
  - Set GAIN pin for desired volume

### 2. Upload the Sketch

1. Open `record_play_loop.ino` in Arduino IDE
2. Select **Board**: ESP32S3 Dev Module
3. Select **Partition Scheme**: 16MB Flash (3MB APP/9MB FATFS)
4. Select **PSRAM**: OPI PSRAM
5. Upload

### 3. Monitor Operation

Open Serial Monitor at **115200 baud**:

\```

### 4. LED Feedback

- **Blinking**: Recording in progress
- **Solid ON**: Playback running

## Testing Tips

### Test Recording Quality

During the 30-second recording:
- Speak clearly from different positions
- Tap near each microphone to verify both are working
- Try speaking while moving between mics

### Test Playback Volume

If playback is too quiet or too loud:

**Hardware adjustments:**
- **GAIN pin**: Float (9dB), GND (12dB), or VDD (15dB)
- **Power**: 5V gives more power than 3.3V
- **Speaker**: 4-ohm speakers are louder than 8-ohm

**Code adjustments (if needed):**
\```cpp
// In playMonoBuffer(), scale samples before writing:
int16_t scaled = mono_buffer[i] * 2;  // 2x gain (may clip!)
i2s_write(I2S_NUM_1, &scaled, ...);
\```

### Test Downmix Quality

The HYBRID algorithm should provide:
- ✅ Clear, intelligible voice
- ✅ Captures from multiple directions
- ✅ No "interruption" when blocking one mic
- ✅ Less background noise than simple average

## Troubleshooting

### No audio from speaker

- Check MAX98357A wiring (especially BCLK, LRC, DIN)
- Verify speaker is connected to SPK+/SPK-
- Try connecting SD pin to VIN (enable amplifier)
- Check Serial Monitor for I2S1 initialization errors

### Distorted/clipped audio

- Lower GAIN pin setting (try Float = 9dB)
- Check speaker impedance (4-8 ohm required)
- Verify 5V power is stable

### Quiet playback

- Increase GAIN pin setting (connect to VDD = 15dB)
- Use 5V instead of 3.3V for VIN
- Use 4-ohm speaker instead of 8-ohm

### Recording noise/static

- Check microphone wiring (especially L/R pins)
- Verify both mics are powered (3.3V to VDD)
- Ensure solid I2S connections (GPIO 2, 4, 18)
- Try different microphones if one is defective

### Playback loops too fast/slow

- Sample rate mismatch - ensure both I2S buses use 16kHz
- Check `SAMPLE_RATE` constant is 16000

## How It Works

### 1. Dual I2S Buses

ESP32-S3 has multiple I2S peripherals:
- **I2S_NUM_0**: Microphones (RX mode)
- **I2S_NUM_1**: Speaker (TX mode)

These run independently and can operate simultaneously.

### 2. Recording Phase

\```
I2S0 (mics) → i2s_buffer (32-bit) → stereo_buffer (16-bit, PSRAM)
\```

Captures 30 seconds of stereo audio (left + right interleaved).

### 3. Downmix Phase

\```
stereo_buffer → HYBRID algorithm → mono_buffer (PSRAM)
\```

Applies adaptive weighting with 30%-70% constraints.

### 4. Playback Phase

\```
mono_buffer → I2S1 (speaker) → Loop forever
\```

Continuously plays the mono recording.

## Next Steps

Once you've verified the basic loop works:

1. **Add voice activity detection (VAD)** - Only record when voice detected
2. **Implement push-to-talk** - Button to trigger recording
3. **Add effects** - Reverb, echo, pitch shift
4. **Stream to WiFi** - Send audio over network
5. **Add compression** - OPUS codec for smaller files
6. **Dual direction** - Record while playing (walkie-talkie mode)

## Technical References

- **ESP32-S3 I2S**: [ESP-IDF I2S Documentation](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/latest/esp32s3/api-reference/peripherals/i2s.html)
- **INMP441 Datasheet**: Omnidirectional I2S MEMS Microphone
- **MAX98357A Datasheet**: I2S Class D Amplifier
- **Hybrid Downmix**: Adaptive weighting with minimum contribution per channel

---

**Power Tip:** For battery operation, use 3.3V for MAX98357A VIN to reduce current draw. Volume will be lower but adequate for close listening!

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929)**_

Good question! Let me help you identify the USB wires safely with your multimeter.

## USB Wire Color Standard

Most USB cables follow this color code:
- **Red** → **+5V** (positive/VCC/VBUS)
- **Black** → **Ground** (negative/GND)
- **White** → Data- (not needed for power)
- **Green** → Data+ (not needed for power)

**For the MAX98357A, you only need Red (+5V) and Black (GND).**

## Multimeter Setup

Here's how to configure your multimeter to test voltage:

### 1. **Probe Connections**
```
Black probe → COM port (common/ground)
Red probe   → V/Ω port (voltage/resistance)
```

### 2. **Knob Setting**
Turn the knob to **DC Voltage** (look for):
- Symbol: **V⎓** or **VDC** or **V—** (V with straight line)
- Range: **20V** (if your meter has multiple voltage ranges)

**Important:** Use DC, NOT AC! AC is usually marked with **V~** or **VAC**.

## Testing Procedure

### Safety First!
Before connecting anything to your ESP32:

1. **Plug in the USB cable** to your 5V battery pack
2. **Touch the probes** to different wire combinations
3. **Look for +5V reading** on the display

### Step-by-Step Testing

```
Step 1: Find the positive wire
─────────────────────────────
Black probe → Touch to BLACK wire (assumed ground)
Red probe   → Touch to RED wire

Expected reading: +4.5V to +5.2V ✓

If you see:
  +5V  → Red is positive, Black is ground ✓
  -5V  → Red is ground, Black is positive (swap understanding)
   0V  → Try different wire combination
```

```
Step 2: Verify ground (optional)
────────────────────────────────
Black probe → Touch to RED wire
Red probe   → Touch to BLACK wire

Expected reading: -4.5V to -5.2V
(This confirms the polarity is reversed)
```

```
Step 3: Ignore data wires
─────────────────────────
White and Green wires will show:
  - 0V or very low voltage (< 1V) when measured against ground
  - These are for USB data communication
  - You don't need them for power!
```

## What You Should See

| Wire Color | Function | Voltage vs Black Wire |
|------------|----------|----------------------|
| **Red**    | +5V      | **+5.0V** ← Use this for VIN |
| **Black**  | GND      | **0.0V** ← Use this for GND |
| White      | Data-    | ~0V (ignore) |
| Green      | Data+    | ~0V (ignore) |

## Quick Reference Card

Print or save this:

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════╗
║  MULTIMETER QUICK SETUP (DC VOLTAGE) ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════╣
║  1. Knob → V⎓ or VDC (20V range)     ║
║  2. Black probe → COM port           ║
║  3. Red probe → V/Ω port             ║
║  4. Test: Black→BLACK, Red→RED wire  ║
║  5. Should read: ~5.0V               ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════╝
```

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

❌ **Don't set to AC voltage** (V~ symbol) - you'll get wrong/zero readings  
❌ **Don't set to resistance** (Ω symbol) - can damage meter when powered  
❌ **Don't short wires together** - will drain battery fast  
❌ **Don't touch probe tips together** while connected - creates short circuit

## If You're Still Unsure

**Safest method** if you can't identify colors:

1. Set multimeter to DC 20V
2. Touch black probe to ONE wire (hold it there)
3. Touch red probe to EACH of the other wires one by one
4. The combination that gives **+5V** is your answer:
   - Wire touching BLACK probe = GND
   - Wire touching RED probe = +5V

## Connecting to MAX98357A

Once identified:

```
USB Cable          MAX98357A
─────────────      ──────────
RED wire    ────→  VIN (+5V)
BLACK wire  ────→  GND
WHITE wire  ────→  (not connected)
GREEN wire  ────→  (not connected)
```

## Verification Before Connecting ESP32

Before wiring everything together:

1. **Measure the voltage** between Red and Black wires: Should be **4.8V - 5.2V**
2. If it's **way higher** (like 12V or 19V), your regulator might be faulty!
3. If it's **correct**, you're good to connect to MAX98357A VIN

## Pro Tip

Once you identify the wires, use a marker or tape to label them:
- Red wire → Write "+" or "+5V"
- Black wire → Write "-" or "GND"

This way you never have to test again!

2. Power both the ESP32 and MAX98357A from the same power bank
3. Use a different power source without load detection
4. Use a power bank that supports low-current mode

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929)**_

This is a classic **USB power bank auto-shutoff** problem! The regulator has a minimum load detection circuit, and the MAX98357A alone doesn't draw enough current when idle/quiet, so it thinks nothing is connected and shuts down.

## Quick Solutions

### **Option 1: Power Everything from One Source (Recommended)**

Instead of splitting the power, connect like this:

```
18650 cell with 5V regulator
         │
         ├─→ ESP32 USB-C port (powers ESP32 + provides 5V rail)
         └─→ MAX98357A VIN ──→ Connect to ESP32's 5V pin
```

The ESP32-S3-LCD-2 has a **5V rail** available. Looking at the schematic, you can:
- Power the ESP32 via USB-C from your 18650 power bank
- Connect MAX98357A's VIN to the **5V pin** on the ESP32 header

This way the ESP32 provides the minimum load to keep the power bank alive, and the MAX98357A shares the same 5V rail.

### **Option 2: Add a Dummy Load Resistor**

If you want to keep them separate, add a resistor across the 5V output to draw ~100mA:

```
5V ────┬──── MAX98357A VIN
       │
       └──── [50Ω 1W resistor] ──── GND

Power = V²/R = 25/50 = 0.5W (use 1W resistor for safety)
Current = V/R = 5/50 = 100mA
```

This wastes power but keeps the regulator alive.

### **Option 3: Use ESP32's 5V Pin**

Check if your ESP32 board has a **5V** pin broken out to the headers. From the schematic, pin headers P1/P2 might have 5V available. If so:

```
18650 → ESP32 USB-C (or 5V pin)
              │
              └─→ ESP32 5V pin → MAX98357A VIN
```

## Why This Happens

USB power banks have load detection to save battery:
- Minimum current: Usually 50-100mA
- MAX98357A idle: ~10-20mA (too low!)
- ESP32 running: ~80-200mA (enough to keep regulator on)

## My Recommendation

**Power both from the same source** - connect your 18650's USB output to the ESP32's USB-C port, then connect MAX98357A's VIN to the ESP32's 5V output. This is cleanest and most efficient.

Let me know which pins are broken out on your board and I can tell you exactly where to connect!

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929)**_

Great that you're getting sound! The quiet volume is likely due to **impedance** and **GAIN settings**. Let's fix it.

## Speaker Connection: **PARALLEL** (for maximum volume)

Connect your two speakers in **PARALLEL** to the MAX98357A:

```
MAX98357A:
  SPK+ ───┬──── Speaker 1 (+)
          └──── Speaker 2 (+)
  
  SPK- ───┬──── Speaker 1 (-)
          └──── Speaker 2 (-)
```

### Why Parallel?

If each speaker is 8Ω:
- **Parallel**: 8Ω || 8Ω = **4Ω total** → LOUDER (more current, more power)
- **Series**: 8Ω + 8Ω = **16Ω total** → quieter (less current)

The MAX98357A outputs **maximum power into 4Ω loads**, so parallel is better for volume.

## Hardware: Set GAIN to Maximum

On the MAX98357A module, the **GAIN pin** controls volume:

| GAIN Pin      | Gain  | Volume |
|---------------|-------|--------|
| Float (unconnected) | 9dB   | Quietest |
| Connect to GND | 12dB  | Medium |
| **Connect to VDD** | **15dB** | **LOUDEST** |

**Connect GAIN pin to VDD (3.3V or 5V)** for maximum hardware gain.

The recording might be at low volume. Let's add software gain to the playback:

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929)**_

No, **NOT a GPIO!** The GAIN pin goes directly to **power** (3.3V or 5V), not to a GPIO pin.

## GAIN Pin Connection (for loudest volume):

```
MAX98357A GAIN pin → Connect to 3.3V or 5V pin on ESP32
```

The GAIN pin is a **hardware configuration pin**, not a control signal. It sets the amplifier's gain based on the voltage it sees:

| Connect GAIN to | Voltage | Gain | Volume |
|-----------------|---------|------|--------|
| **Nothing (float)** | ~1.6V | 9dB  | Quiet  |
| **GND** | 0V | 12dB | Medium |
| **VDD (3.3V or 5V)** | 3.3V/5V | **15dB** | **LOUDEST** |

## Easiest Way:

Since you're already powering the MAX98357A from the ESP32's 5V pin, just connect:

```
ESP32 5V pin ───┬─→ MAX98357A VIN
                └─→ MAX98357A GAIN  (for maximum volume!)
```

So **both VIN and GAIN** connect to the same 5V source. This gives you maximum hardware gain (15dB).

## Summary of ALL Connections:

```
ESP32 → MAX98357A
─────────────────
5V    → VIN
5V    → GAIN (for loudest!)
GND   → GND
GPIO6 → BCLK
GPIO7 → LRC
GPIO8 → DIN
```

No GPIO needed for GAIN - it's just a voltage reference pin! Upload the updated code and you should get really loud audio now. 🔊

/*
 * MAX98357A Speaker Beep Test
 *
 * Simple test that plays beeps and boops to verify speaker hardware.
 * Plays a sequence of tones at different frequencies.
 *
 * Hardware Wiring:
 * ================
 * MAX98357A → ESP32-S3-LCD-2
 * ─────────────────────────
 * VIN   → 5V
 * GND   → GND
 * BCLK  → GPIO 6
 * LRC   → GPIO 7
 * DIN   → GPIO 8
 * GAIN  → 5V (for maximum volume) or Float (for 9dB)
 * SD    → VIN (always on)
 *
 * Speakers:
 * ─────────
 * SPK+ ───┬──── Speaker 1 (+)
 *         └──── Speaker 2 (+)
 *
 * SPK- ───┬──── Speaker 1 (-)
 *         └──── Speaker 2 (-)
 *
 * Expected Output:
 * ================
 * You should hear a sequence of beeps cycling through:
 * - 440 Hz (A note - musical A)
 * - 523 Hz (C note)
 * - 659 Hz (E note)
 * - 784 Hz (G note)
 * Then a rising sweep from 200 Hz to 2000 Hz
 *
 * If you hear this clearly, your speaker hardware is working!
 */

#include <driver/i2s.h>
#include <math.h>

// Speaker pins (I2S1)
#define SPK_BCK_PIN    6
#define SPK_WS_PIN     7
#define SPK_DOUT_PIN   8

// Audio config
#define I2S_PORT       I2S_NUM_1
#define SAMPLE_RATE    16000
#define BUFFER_SIZE    512

// LED for feedback
#define LED_PIN 1

int16_t audio_buffer[BUFFER_SIZE];

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(1000);

  pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);

  Serial.println("\n========================================");
  Serial.println("MAX98357A Speaker Beep Test");
  Serial.println("========================================\n");
  Serial.printf("Pins: BCK=%d, WS=%d, DOUT=%d\n\n", SPK_BCK_PIN, SPK_WS_PIN, SPK_DOUT_PIN);

  // Initialize I2S
  Serial.print("Initializing I2S... ");
  i2s_config_t i2s_config = {
    .mode = (i2s_mode_t)(I2S_MODE_MASTER | I2S_MODE_TX),
    .sample_rate = SAMPLE_RATE,
    .bits_per_sample = I2S_BITS_PER_SAMPLE_16BIT,
    .channel_format = I2S_CHANNEL_FMT_ONLY_LEFT,  // Mono
    .communication_format = I2S_COMM_FORMAT_STAND_I2S,
    .intr_alloc_flags = ESP_INTR_FLAG_LEVEL1,
    .dma_buf_count = 4,
    .dma_buf_len = 512,
    .use_apll = false,
    .tx_desc_auto_clear = true,
    .fixed_mclk = 0
  };

  i2s_pin_config_t pin_config = {
    .bck_io_num = SPK_BCK_PIN,
    .ws_io_num = SPK_WS_PIN,
    .data_out_num = SPK_DOUT_PIN,
    .data_in_num = I2S_PIN_NO_CHANGE
  };

  if (i2s_driver_install(I2S_PORT, &i2s_config, 0, NULL) != ESP_OK ||
      i2s_set_pin(I2S_PORT, &pin_config) != ESP_OK) {
    Serial.println("FAILED");
    Serial.println("ERROR: I2S initialization failed!");
    while(1) {
      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, !digitalRead(LED_PIN));
      delay(200);
    }
  }
  Serial.println("OK\n");

  Serial.println("========================================");
  Serial.println("Playing test tones...");
  Serial.println("========================================\n");
  Serial.println("You should hear:");
  Serial.println("  1. Four musical notes (A, C, E, G)");
  Serial.println("  2. A rising sweep (200-2000 Hz)");
  Serial.println("  3. Pattern repeats forever\n");

  delay(500);
}

void loop() {
  // Play sequence of musical notes
  playTone(440, 500);  // A note
  delay(100);

  playTone(523, 500);  // C note
  delay(100);

  playTone(659, 500);  // E note
  delay(100);

  playTone(784, 500);  // G note
  delay(100);

  // Rising sweep
  Serial.println("Playing sweep 200-2000 Hz...");
  for (int freq = 200; freq <= 2000; freq += 50) {
    playTone(freq, 50);
  }

  delay(1000);
  Serial.println("Repeating test sequence...\n");
}

void playTone(float frequency, int duration_ms) {
  Serial.printf("Playing %d Hz for %d ms\n", (int)frequency, duration_ms);

  unsigned long start = millis();
  int samples_sent = 0;

  while (millis() - start < duration_ms) {
    // Generate sine wave samples
    for (int i = 0; i < BUFFER_SIZE; i++) {
      float t = (float)(samples_sent + i) / SAMPLE_RATE;
      float sample = sin(2.0 * PI * frequency * t);

      // Convert to 16-bit with 50% volume (to prevent clipping)
      audio_buffer[i] = (int16_t)(sample * 16000);
    }

    // Send to speaker
    size_t bytes_written;
    i2s_write(I2S_PORT, audio_buffer, BUFFER_SIZE * sizeof(int16_t), &bytes_written, portMAX_DELAY);

    samples_sent += BUFFER_SIZE;

    // Blink LED while playing
    if ((millis() / 100) % 2 == 0) {
      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
    } else {
      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
    }
  }
}

# Speaker Beep Test

## What This Does

This is a **hardware verification test** for your MAX98357A amplifier and speakers. It plays simple beeps and tones so you can confirm everything is wired correctly.

## What You Should Hear

If everything is working, you'll hear:

1. **Four musical notes** (A, C, E, G) - short beeps
2. **A rising sweep** from low to high pitch (200 Hz → 2000 Hz)
3. **Pattern repeats** forever

## Wiring (Same as Before)

\```
MAX98357A → ESP32
─────────────────
VIN   → 5V
GND   → GND
BCLK  → GPIO 6
LRC   → GPIO 7
DIN   → GPIO 8
GAIN  → 5V (loud) or Float (quieter) or GND (medium)

Speakers (PARALLEL):
SPK+ ───┬──── Speaker 1 (+)
        └──── Speaker 2 (+)

SPK- ───┬──── Speaker 1 (-)
        └──── Speaker 2 (-)
\```

## Upload and Test

1. Open `speaker_beep_test.ino` in Arduino IDE
2. Upload to ESP32
3. Open Serial Monitor (115200 baud)
4. **Listen for beeps!**

## Troubleshooting

### ❌ I hear NOTHING

**Check wiring:**
- GPIO 6 → BCLK (not DIN!)
- GPIO 7 → LRC (not BCLK!)
- GPIO 8 → DIN (not LRC!)
- 5V → VIN (power)
- GND → GND

**Check speakers:**
- SPK+ and SPK- connected?
- Speakers in parallel (not series)?
- Speaker wires not touching/shorting?

**Check Serial Monitor:**
- Does it say "Initializing I2S... OK"?
- If it says "FAILED", there's an I2S problem

### ❌ Very quiet / barely audible

**Try this:**
1. **Disconnect GAIN pin** (leave it floating) - see if you hear anything
2. **Connect GAIN to GND** - should be medium volume
3. **Connect GAIN to 5V** - should be loudest

If you still can't hear anything even at maximum GAIN, check:
- Speaker impedance (should be 4-8 ohm)
- Speaker is not broken (test with another device)
- MAX98357A board is not damaged

### ❌ Distorted / crackling

- Lower the GAIN pin (try Float or GND instead of 5V)
- Check speaker impedance (might be too low, like 2 ohm)
- Verify 5V power supply can provide enough current

### ✅ I hear clear beeps!

**Your speaker hardware is PERFECT!** The problem was with the recording/playback sketch, not the hardware. Possible issues with the original sketch:
1. Recording didn't work (mic issue)
2. Downmix had a bug
3. Playback buffer was empty

Go back to the `record_play_loop` sketch and check the Serial Monitor during recording to see where it failed.

## What the Test Proves

If this test works:
- ✅ MAX98357A is working
- ✅ I2S1 peripheral is configured correctly
- ✅ Speakers are wired correctly
- ✅ GPIO pins 6, 7, 8 are functional
- ✅ Power supply is adequate

The issue is NOT with your speaker hardware!

## Next Steps

Once you confirm this test works:
1. Go back to `record_play_loop` sketch
2. Connect to USB and check Serial Monitor
3. Look for which step fails:
   - Recording? (mic issue)
   - Downmix? (algorithm issue)
   - Playback? (buffer issue)

Let me know what you hear and we'll fix the recording sketch!

Summary:
## 1. Primary Request and Intent

User requested a new sketch that combines dual INMP441 microphone recording with MAX98357A speaker playback:
- **Record 30 seconds** of stereo audio from two INMP441 microphones
- **Downmix to mono** using the HYBRID algorithm (previously developed and tested)
- **Play back** the mono audio through MAX98357A amplifier with 2x 1W flat mag speakers
- **Determine pin configuration** from ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-2 schematic
- **Maximize volume** for good sound quality

User also wanted to test speaker hardware independently when main sketch had volume issues, and requested documentation updates for future reference.

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

- **Dual I2S Buses on ESP32-S3**: I2S_NUM_0 (microphones, RX mode) and I2S_NUM_1 (speaker, TX mode) operating simultaneously
- **INMP441 MEMS Microphones**: I2S digital microphones with L/R channel selection via hardware pin (L/R→GND=LEFT, L/R→VDD=RIGHT)
- **MAX98357A I2S Class-D Amplifier**: Hardware GAIN pin controls amplification (Float=9dB, GND=12dB, VDD=15dB)
- **HYBRID Downmix Algorithm**: Adaptive weighting with 30%-70% constraints for clarity + width
- **PSRAM Buffering**: Store entire recording before playback to avoid SD card timing issues
- **Audio Normalization**: Automatic peak detection and gain adjustment to maximize playback volume
- **Speaker Impedance**: Parallel connection of 8Ω speakers = 4Ω total (optimal for MAX98357A)
- **USB Power Bank Auto-Shutoff**: Minimum load detection requires sufficient current draw
- **Software Gain Compensation**: Digital amplification to compensate for limited hardware gain

## 3. Files and Code Sections

### `/home/alphons/project/OAISYS25/badge/workbench/docs/ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-2-SchDoc.pdf`
- **Why examined**: To identify available GPIO pins for MAX98357A connection
- **Key findings**: GPIO 6, 7, 8 are camera pins (safe when no camera attached), confirmed from PinOut section

### `/home/alphons/project/OAISYS25/badge/workbench/tests/speaker_test/speaker_test.ino`
- **Why examined**: Reference for MAX98357A I2S configuration and pin usage
- **Key details**: Already used GPIO 6, 7, 8 for I2S1 speaker output

1. **Added software gain boost** (first iteration):

// In downmix loop:

if (mixed > 32767) mixed = 32767;
if (mixed < -32768) mixed = -32768;
mono_buffer[i] = (int16_t)mixed;
```

2. **Reduced gain after testing**:
```cpp

```

3. **Increased gain for final version**:
```cpp
const float GAIN_BOOST = 4.0f;   // 4x volume boost (compensates for 9dB hardware gain)
```

4. **Added automatic normalization function**:
```cpp
void normalizeAudio() {
  // Find peak level in recording
  int16_t peak = 0;
  for (uint32_t i = 0; i < MONO_SAMPLES; i++) {
    int16_t abs_val = abs(mono_buffer[i]);
    if (abs_val > peak) peak = abs_val;
  }

  Serial.printf("Peak level: %d / 32767 (%.1f%%)\n", peak, (peak * 100.0f) / 32767.0f);

  // Calculate normalization gain to maximize volume
  if (peak > 0) {
    float norm_gain = 32000.0f / peak;  // Leave small headroom
    if (norm_gain > 8.0f) norm_gain = 8.0f;  // Limit max boost

    Serial.printf("Applying normalization: %.2fx gain\n", norm_gain);

    // Apply normalization
    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < MONO_SAMPLES; i++) {
      int32_t normalized = (int32_t)(mono_buffer[i] * norm_gain);
      if (normalized > 32767) normalized = 32767;
      if (normalized < -32768) normalized = -32768;
      mono_buffer[i] = (int16_t)normalized;
    }
  } else {
    Serial.println("WARNING: Recording is silent (peak = 0)!");
  }
}
```

5. **Integrated normalization into setup**:
```cpp
// Downmix to mono using HYBRID
Serial.print("Applying HYBRID downmix... ");
downmixHybrid();
Serial.println("OK");

// Analyze and normalize
normalizeAudio();
Serial.println();
```

### `/home/alphons/project/OAISYS25/badge/workbench/tests/speaker_beep_test/speaker_beep_test.ino`
- **Why created**: Hardware verification test to isolate MAX98357A and speaker issues from recording/playback problems
- **Purpose**: Plays musical tones (A, C, E, G notes) and frequency sweep to verify speaker hardware works
```cpp
void playTone(float frequency, int duration_ms) {
  unsigned long start = millis();
  int samples_sent = 0;

  while (millis() - start < duration_ms) {
    // Generate sine wave samples
    for (int i = 0; i < BUFFER_SIZE; i++) {
      float t = (float)(samples_sent + i) / SAMPLE_RATE;
      float sample = sin(2.0 * PI * frequency * t);
      audio_buffer[i] = (int16_t)(sample * 16000);  // 50% volume
    }

    size_t bytes_written;
    i2s_write(I2S_PORT, audio_buffer, BUFFER_SIZE * sizeof(int16_t), &bytes_written, portMAX_DELAY);
    samples_sent += BUFFER_SIZE;
  }
}
```

## 4. Errors and Fixes

### Error 1: USB Power Bank Auto-Shutoff
- **Problem**: User's 18650 cell with 5V regulator shut down when powering MAX98357A via split USB cable
- **Cause**: MAX98357A draws too little current (~10-20mA idle), below regulator's minimum load detection threshold
- **Fix**: User chose Option 3 - power ESP32 via USB-C, then connect MAX98357A VIN to ESP32's 5V pin
- **User feedback**: "I went with option 3"

### Error 2: Very Quiet Audio Initially
- **Problem**: User could hear sound "very lightly" when first testing
- **Cause**: Multiple factors - speaker wiring, GAIN pin not configured, no software gain
- **Fix Applied**:
  1. Advised parallel speaker connection (4Ω impedance)
  2. Recommended GAIN pin to VDD (15dB)
  3. Added software gain boost (GAIN_BOOST = 3.0f) with clipping protection
- **User feedback**: "ohkay I am a little confused where should i connec the audio boards gain pin too?"

### Error 3: No Sound After GAIN Pin Connection
- **Problem**: After connecting GAIN to 5V as instructed, user got zero sound (only "very quiet white noise")
- **Cause**: Unknown hardware issue with GAIN pin connection to 5V
- **Troubleshooting approach**: Created speaker_beep_test to isolate hardware
- **User feedback**: "I did the connection like you said but now there is 0 sound"

### Error 4: GAIN Pin Only Works When Floating
- **Problem**: Hardware only produces sound when GAIN pin is disconnected (floating = 9dB), not when connected to 5V or GND
- **Root cause**: Possible MAX98357A module issue or incompatibility with board
- **Fix**: Compensate with aggressive software gain instead of hardware gain
  - Increased GAIN_BOOST to 4.0f
  - Added normalizeAudio() for up to 8x additional boost
  - Total possible gain: 4x × 8x = 32x
- **User feedback**: "its only working without the gain pin connected anywhere, we need to pump up the output sound somehow"

### Error 5: Playback Still Quieter Than Expected
- **Problem**: Even with 4x gain + normalization, playback not as loud as beep test
- **Cause**: Beep test generated full-amplitude sine waves (~50% max), while mic recording depends on voice volume and INMP441 sensitivity
- **Status**: User accepted current state - "alright thats a wrap the boost worked a bit not enough, not even loud enough like the beep-boops test we did earlier... But nah thats sort of fine for now"
- **Documentation**: Added notes to README for future improvement (increase GAIN_BOOST to 6-8x, speak louder, position mics closer)

### Solved Problems:

1. **Pin identification for MAX98357A**: Successfully identified GPIO 6, 7, 8 from schematic (camera pins, safe when no camera)

2. **Dual I2S bus configuration**: Implemented simultaneous I2S0 (microphones) and I2S1 (speaker) operation without conflicts

3. **USB power bank auto-shutoff**: Resolved by powering through ESP32 USB-C, using ESP32's 5V output for MAX98357A

4. **Speaker wiring for maximum volume**: Determined parallel connection (4Ω total) is optimal for MAX98357A

5. **Hardware gain limitation**: When GAIN pin couldn't be used, compensated with software gain (4x) + normalization (up to 8x)

   194→bool recordStereoToPSRAM() {
   195→  uint32_t samples_written = 0;
   196→  uint32_t last_percent = 0;

   201→    if ((millis() / 200) % 2 == 0) {
   202→      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, HIGH);
   203→    } else {
   204→      digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
   205→    }
   206→
   207→    // Read I2S
   208→    size_t bytes_read = 0;
   209→    if (i2s_read(I2S_NUM_0, i2s_buffer, BUFFER_SIZE * sizeof(int32_t),
   210→                 &bytes_read, portMAX_DELAY) != ESP_OK) {
   211→      return false;
   212→    }
   213→
   214→    // Convert and store
   215→    int samples_read = bytes_read / sizeof(int32_t);
   216→    for (int i = 0; i < samples_read && samples_written < STEREO_SAMPLES; i++) {
   217→      stereo_buffer[samples_written++] = (int16_t)(i2s_buffer[i] >> 16);
   218→    }
   219→
   220→    // Progress
   221→    uint32_t percent = (samples_written * 100) / STEREO_SAMPLES;
   222→    if (percent != last_percent && percent % 10 == 0) {
   223→      Serial.printf("Progress: %u%% (%u / %u samples)\n",
   224→                    percent, samples_written, STEREO_SAMPLES);
   225→      last_percent = percent;
   226→    }
   227→  }
   228→
   229→  Serial.printf("\nRecorded: %u samples in %lu ms\n", samples_written, millis() - start_time);
   230→  return true;
   231→}

   233→void downmixHybrid() {
   234→  float left_energy = 0.0f;
   235→  float right_energy = 0.0f;
   236→  const float ENERGY_DECAY = 0.95f;
   237→  const float MIN_WEIGHT = 0.30f;  // Minimum 30% per channel
   238→  const float MAX_WEIGHT = 0.70f;  // Maximum 70% per channel
   239→  const float GAIN_BOOST = 4.0f;   // 4x volume boost (compensates for 9dB hardware gain)
   240→
   241→  for (uint32_t i = 0; i < MONO_SAMPLES; i++) {
   242→    int16_t left = stereo_buffer[i * 2];
   243→    int16_t right = stereo_buffer[i * 2 + 1];
   244→
   245→    // Track energy of each channel
   246→    left_energy = left_energy * ENERGY_DECAY + abs(left) * (1.0f - ENERGY_DECAY);
   247→    right_energy = right_energy * ENERGY_DECAY + abs(right) * (1.0f - ENERGY_DECAY);
   248→
   249→    // Calculate raw weights
   250→    float total_energy = left_energy + right_energy;
   251→    float left_weight = (total_energy > 0) ? (left_energy / total_energy) : 0.5f;
   252→
   253→    // Constrain to 30%-70% range
   254→    if (left_weight < MIN_WEIGHT) left_weight = MIN_WEIGHT;
   255→    if (left_weight > MAX_WEIGHT) left_weight = MAX_WEIGHT;
   256→
   257→    float right_weight = 1.0f - left_weight;
   258→
   259→    // Weighted mix with gain boost and clipping protection
   260→    int32_t mixed = (int32_t)(left * left_weight + right * right_weight) * GAIN_BOOST;
   261→    if (mixed > 32767) mixed = 32767;
   262→    if (mixed < -32768) mixed = -32768;
   263→    mono_buffer[i] = (int16_t)mixed;
   264→  }
   265→}
   266→
   267→void normalizeAudio() {
   268→  // Find peak level in recording
   269→  int16_t peak = 0;
   270→  for (uint32_t i = 0; i < MONO_SAMPLES; i++) {
   271→    int16_t abs_val = abs(mono_buffer[i]);
   272→    if (abs_val > peak) peak = abs_val;
   273→  }
   274→
   275→  Serial.printf("Peak level: %d / 32767 (%.1f%%)\n", peak, (peak * 100.0f) / 32767.0f);
   276→
   277→  // Calculate normalization gain to maximize volume
   278→  if (peak > 0) {
   279→    float norm_gain = 32000.0f / peak;  // Leave small headroom (32000 instead of 32767)
   280→
   281→    // Limit max boost to 8x to avoid amplifying noise too much
   282→    if (norm_gain > 8.0f) norm_gain = 8.0f;
   283→
   284→    Serial.printf("Applying normalization: %.2fx gain\n", norm_gain);
   285→
   286→    // Apply normalization
   287→    for (uint32_t i = 0; i < MONO_SAMPLES; i++) {
   288→      int32_t normalized = (int32_t)(mono_buffer[i] * norm_gain);
   289→      if (normalized > 32767) normalized = 32767;
   290→      if (normalized < -32768) normalized = -32768;
   291→      mono_buffer[i] = (int16_t)normalized;
   292→    }
   293→  } else {
   294→    Serial.println("WARNING: Recording is silent (peak = 0)!");
   295→  }
   296→}
   297→
   298→void playMonoBuffer() {
   299→  size_t bytes_written = 0;
   300→  static unsigned long last_print = 0;
   301→
   302→  // Play entire mono buffer
   303→  for (uint32_t i = 0; i < MONO_SAMPLES; i += BUFFER_SIZE) {
   304→    uint32_t samples_to_write = min((uint32_t)BUFFER_SIZE, MONO_SAMPLES - i);
   305→
   306→    i2s_write(I2S_NUM_1, &mono_buffer[i], samples_to_write * sizeof(int16_t),
   307→              &bytes_written, portMAX_DELAY);
   308→
   309→    // Print status every ~2 seconds
   310→    if (millis() - last_print > 2000) {
   311→      Serial.printf("Playing... sample %u / %u\n", i, MONO_SAMPLES);
   312→      last_print = millis();
   313→    }
   314→  }
   315→
   316→  Serial.println("Playback complete, looping...\n");
   317→}
   318→
   319→void error_blink() {
   320→  while(1) {
   321→    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, !digitalRead(LED_PIN));
   322→    delay(200);
   323→  }
   324→}

     1→# Record, Downmix, and Playback Loop
     2→
     3→## Overview
     4→
     5→This sketch demonstrates a complete audio capture and playback pipeline:
     6→1. **Records 30 seconds** of stereo audio from dual INMP441 microphones
     7→2. **Downmixes to mono** using HYBRID algorithm (adaptive + width)
     8→3. **Plays back** continuously through MAX98357A speaker
     9→
    10→## Hardware Requirements
    11→
    12→- ESP32-S3-LCD-2 board
    13→- 2× INMP441 MEMS microphones
    14→- 1× MAX98357A I2S amplifier module
    15→- 2× 1W flat mag speakers (4-8 ohm)
    16→- Breadboard and jumper wires
    17→
    18→## Wiring Diagram
    19→
    20→### INMP441 Microphones → ESP32 (I2S0)
    21→
    22→```

    24→────────────────        ─────────────────      ──────────────────
    25→3.3V ───────────┬────── VDD                    VDD
    26→                │
    27→GND ────────────┼────── GND ──────────┬─────── GND
    28→                │                     │
    29→GPIO 2 (BCK) ───┼────── SCK ──────────┼─────── SCK
    30→GPIO 4 (WS) ────┼────── WS ───────────┼─────── WS
    31→GPIO 18 (DIN) ──┴────── SD ───────────┴─────── SD
    32→                        │                      │
    33→                        L/R → GND              L/R → 3.3V
    34→                          (LEFT)                 (RIGHT)
    35→```
    36→
    37→### MAX98357A Speaker → ESP32 (I2S1)
    38→
    39→```
    40→MAX98357A               ESP32-S3-LCD-2
    41→─────────────           ────────────────
    42→VIN    ─────────────────→ 5V (or 3.3V)
    43→GND    ─────────────────→ GND
    44→BCLK   ─────────────────→ GPIO 6
    45→LRC    ─────────────────→ GPIO 7
    46→DIN    ─────────────────→ GPIO 8
    47→GAIN   ─────────────────→ Float (9dB) / GND (12dB) / VDD (15dB)
    48→SD     ─────────────────→ VIN (always on)
    49→
    50→SPK+   ─────────────────→ Speaker +
    51→SPK-   ─────────────────→ Speaker -
    52→```
    53→
    54→## Pin Summary
    55→

    57→|---------------|-----------|----------------|--------------------------------|

    64→| **Speaker (I2S1)** |           |                |                                |

    72→## Audio Specifications

    82→
    83→## Downmix Algorithm: HYBRID
    84→
    85→The HYBRID downmix algorithm combines the best of two approaches:
    86→
    87→- **Adaptive weighting**: Favors the microphone with stronger signal (clarity)
    88→- **30%-70% constraint**: Ensures both channels always contribute (width)
    89→
    90→This prevents the "interruption" feeling when blocking one mic while maintaining clarity and reducing background noise compared to simple averaging.
    91→
    92→## Usage Instructions
    93→
    94→### 1. Wire Everything
    95→
    96→Follow the wiring diagrams above. Critical points:
    97→
    98→- **Microphones**: Both share I2S bus (GPIO 2, 4, 18)
    99→  - Mic #1: L/R → **GND** (left channel)
   100→  - Mic #2: L/R → **3.3V** (right channel)
   101→
   102→- **Speaker**: Connect to I2S1 (GPIO 6, 7, 8)
   103→  - Use **5V** for full power (3.3V works but quieter)
   104→  - Connect speaker to SPK+ and SPK-
   105→  - Set GAIN pin for desired volume
   106→
   107→### 2. Upload the Sketch
   108→
   109→1. Open `record_play_loop.ino` in Arduino IDE
   110→2. Select **Board**: ESP32S3 Dev Module
   111→3. Select **Partition Scheme**: 16MB Flash (3MB APP/9MB FATFS)
   112→4. Select **PSRAM**: OPI PSRAM
   113→5. Upload
   114→
   115→### 3. Monitor Operation
   116→
   117→Open Serial Monitor at **115200 baud**:
   118→
   119→```

   157→
   158→### 4. LED Feedback
   159→
   160→- **Blinking**: Recording in progress
   161→- **Solid ON**: Playback running
   162→
   163→## Testing Tips
   164→
   165→### Test Recording Quality
   166→
   167→During the 30-second recording:
   168→- Speak clearly from different positions
   169→- Tap near each microphone to verify both are working
   170→- Try speaking while moving between mics
   171→
   172→### Test Playback Volume
   173→
   174→If playback is too quiet or too loud:
   175→
   176→**Hardware adjustments:**
   177→- **GAIN pin**: Float (9dB), GND (12dB), or VDD (15dB)
   178→- **Power**: 5V gives more power than 3.3V
   179→- **Speaker**: 4-ohm speakers are louder than 8-ohm
   180→
   181→**Code adjustments (if needed):**
   182→```cpp
   183→// In playMonoBuffer(), scale samples before writing:
   184→int16_t scaled = mono_buffer[i] * 2;  // 2x gain (may clip!)
   185→i2s_write(I2S_NUM_1, &scaled, ...);
   186→```
   187→
   188→### Test Downmix Quality
   189→
   190→The HYBRID algorithm should provide:
   191→- ✅ Clear, intelligible voice
   192→- ✅ Captures from multiple directions
   193→- ✅ No "interruption" when blocking one mic
   194→- ✅ Less background noise than simple average
   195→
   196→## Troubleshooting
   197→
   198→### No audio from speaker
   199→
   200→- Check MAX98357A wiring (especially BCLK, LRC, DIN)
   201→- Verify speaker is connected to SPK+/SPK-
   202→- Try connecting SD pin to VIN (enable amplifier)
   203→- Check Serial Monitor for I2S1 initialization errors
   204→
   205→### Distorted/clipped audio
   206→
   207→- Lower GAIN pin setting (try Float = 9dB)
   208→- Check speaker impedance (4-8 ohm required)
   209→- Verify 5V power is stable
   210→
   211→### Quiet playback
   212→
   213→- Increase GAIN pin setting (connect to VDD = 15dB)
   214→- Use 5V instead of 3.3V for VIN
   215→- Use 4-ohm speaker instead of 8-ohm
   216→- **Software gain**: Increase `GAIN_BOOST` to 6.0f or 8.0f (line 235 in .ino)
   217→- **Recording level**: Speak very loudly into mics during recording, position mics 5-10cm from mouth
   218→
   219→### Recording noise/static
   220→
   221→- Check microphone wiring (especially L/R pins)
   222→- Verify both mics are powered (3.3V to VDD)
   223→- Ensure solid I2S connections (GPIO 2, 4, 18)
   224→- Try different microphones if one is defective
   225→
   226→### Playback loops too fast/slow
   227→
   228→- Sample rate mismatch - ensure both I2S buses use 16kHz
   229→- Check `SAMPLE_RATE` constant is 16000
   230→
   231→## How It Works
   232→
   233→### 1. Dual I2S Buses
   234→
   235→ESP32-S3 has multiple I2S peripherals:
   236→- **I2S_NUM_0**: Microphones (RX mode)
   237→- **I2S_NUM_1**: Speaker (TX mode)
   238→
   239→These run independently and can operate simultaneously.
   240→
   241→### 2. Recording Phase
   242→
   243→```
   244→I2S0 (mics) → i2s_buffer (32-bit) → stereo_buffer (16-bit, PSRAM)
   245→```
   246→
   247→Captures 30 seconds of stereo audio (left + right interleaved).
   248→
   249→### 3. Downmix Phase
   250→
   251→```
   252→stereo_buffer → HYBRID algorithm → mono_buffer (PSRAM)
   253→```
   254→
   255→Applies adaptive weighting with 30%-70% constraints.
   256→
   257→### 4. Playback Phase
   258→
   259→```
   260→mono_buffer → I2S1 (speaker) → Loop forever
   261→```
   262→
   263→Continuously plays the mono recording.
   264→
   265→## Next Steps
   266→
   267→Once you've verified the basic loop works:
   268→
   269→1. **Add voice activity detection (VAD)** - Only record when voice detected
   270→2. **Implement push-to-talk** - Button to trigger recording
   271→3. **Add effects** - Reverb, echo, pitch shift
   272→4. **Stream to WiFi** - Send audio over network
   273→5. **Add compression** - OPUS codec for smaller files
   274→6. **Dual direction** - Record while playing (walkie-talkie mode)
   275→

   279→- **INMP441 Datasheet**: Omnidirectional I2S MEMS Microphone
   280→- **MAX98357A Datasheet**: I2S Class D Amplifier
   281→- **Hybrid Downmix**: Adaptive weighting with minimum contribution per channel
   282→

   284→
   285→**Power Tip:** For battery operation, use 3.3V for MAX98357A VIN to reduce current draw. Volume will be lower but adequate for close listening!

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding **YAMNet-1024 TensorFlow Lite Micro ESP32 implementation**:

## Key Findings

### YAMNet-1024 Specifications
YAMNet-1024 has 3.2 million parameters and outputs embedding vectors of size 1024. The model is quantized in int8 using tensorflow lite converter for Yamnet-256, and ONNX quantizer for Yamnet-1024.

### Current Implementation Status

**STM32N6 Implementation:** The original Yamnet (named Yamnet-1024) is provided for use on the STM32N6, which features the ST Neural-ART Accelerator™, an NPU clocked at 1 GHz and providing up to 600 GOPS of processing capabilities with 4.2 Mbytes of contiguous embedded RAM.

**ESP32 Challenges:** Questions have been raised about whether YAMNet can be ported to microcontrollers such as Arduino, STM32xx, ESP32. From discussions, it isn't feasible to use "yamnet.tflite" on a microcontroller like the ESP32-S3.

### TensorFlow Lite Micro on ESP32

While TensorFlow Lite Micro support exists for ESP32 chipsets, and the esp-tflite-micro component provides examples for Espressif Chipsets using ESP-IDF platform, there is **no evidence of successful YAMNet-1024 implementation on ESP32** in the search results.

The ESP32's hardware limitations (typically 520KB SRAM, 4-8MB flash on common variants) compared to YAMNet-1024's 3.2 million parameters and memory requirements appear to be the primary obstacle for direct deployment.

I found relevant information about YAMNet-256 for ESP32 and TensorFlow Lite Micro applications:

## YAMNet-256: Smaller Audio Embedding Model

YAMNet-256 outputs embedding vectors of size 256, which is significantly smaller than the original YAMNet's 1,024-dimensional embeddings.

### Key Features for Microcontrollers:

**Optimized for Embedded Systems**: The custom layers are not included in Yamnet-256 or Yamnet-1024, as STEDGEAI cannot convert them to C code, and more efficient implementations of these operations already exist on microcontrollers.

**Input Format**: Yamnet-256 and Yamnet-1024 expect mel-spectrogram patches of size 64x96, format (n_mels, n_frames) The model is quantized in int8 using tensorflow lite converter for Yamnet-256.

### ESP32 Compatibility:

A plain old ESP32 without extra PS-RAM is enough to "hear" with about 10 inferences per per second. The Tasmota documentation confirms TensorFlow Lite support for ESP32 and ESP32-S3 platforms with optimized kernels.

### Available Datasets:

We provide Yamnet-256s for two different datasets : ESC-10, which is a small research dataset, and FSD50K, a large generalist dataset using the audioset ontology.

The YAMNet-256 model is available through STMicroelectronics on Hugging Face and is specifically designed for resource-constrained microcontroller environments like the ESP32.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding ESP32-S3 audio embedding extraction with TFLite Micro and model size constraints:

## ESP32-S3 Memory Specifications

The ESP32-S3 has 512 KB on-chip SRAM for data and instructions, running at a configurable frequency of up to 240 MHz. However, only about 225KB of SRAM are typically available for the Internal RAM Heap after accounting for system overhead, caches, and application code.

ESP32-S3 has a few hundred kilobytes of internal RAM, and has the ability to use up to 32 MB of virtual addresses for external PSRAM (Pseudostatic RAM) memory. Common configurations include 8MB each of flash and PSRAM.

## Model Size Examples for Audio Applications

For audio applications on microcontrollers:

- The Micro Speech model is less than 20 kB and can recognize 2 keywords, "yes" and "no", from speech data
- A 10 KB model can be trained to recognize various hand gestures
- Audio keyword spotting models are typically ~20–50 KB in size after optimization

Larger models face challenges:
- The yamnet.tflite file is about 3.9M in size, which is quite large for embedded deployment

## Critical Performance Constraints

A ~2 MB model with a tensor arena of about 5 MB ended up using PSRAM, which slows things down significantly. Such large models took about 60 seconds on ESP32 S3 while taking about 50 ms on PC, demonstrating the severe performance penalty.

About 300K of SRAM is typically available that isn't being used, suggesting that models should ideally fit within a few hundred KB to remain in SRAM for acceptable performance.

## Recommendations

For audio embedding extraction on ESP32-S3, you should aim to keep your model and tensor arena small enough to fit primarily in SRAM (targeting under 200-300 KB total) for real-time performance, or accept significant inference latency if using PSRAM for larger models.

# Yamnet-256 Model Overview

## Available Model Files

The repository provides multiple Yamnet-256 variants:
- **ESC-10 dataset**: Float32 and Int8 quantized versions
- **FSD50K dataset**: Models with and without "unknown class" for domestic AED use cases

## Model Sizes

**Yamnet-256 specifications:**
- Parameters: "130 K"
- Weights Flash (Int8): Approximately 135-167 KB depending on variant
- Total Flash requirement: ~192 KB on STM32U5 series

**Yamnet-1024 (larger variant):**
- Parameters: "3.2 M"
- Weights Flash: ~3,450 KB

## Preprocessing Requirements

The models expect pre-processed audio in spectral format. According to the documentation, the original Yamnet "converts waveforms to spectrograms by using an FFT and window size of 25 ms, a hop length of 10ms, and by clipping frequencies between 125 and 7500 Hz."

## Input/Output Specifications

**Input:** "spectrogram patches of 96 frames and 64 mels, of shape (64, 96, 1)"

**Output:** 
- Yamnet-256: embedding vectors of size 256
- Yamnet-1024: embedding vectors of size 1024

Both support automatic classification head addition during transfer learning.

## YAMNet-256 Model Information

The YAMNet-256 model is quantized in int8 using TensorFlow Lite converter. As the default YAMNet is too large to fit on most microcontrollers (over 3M parameters), STMicroelectronics provides a downsized version called YAMNet-256 which outputs embeddings of size 256.

### Model Specifications:
- Expects mel-spectrogram patches of size 64x96, format (n_mels, n_frames)
- Outputs embedding vectors of size 256
- Input shape: (64, 96, 1)

### Available Versions:
STMicroelectronics provides YAMNet-256 models for two different datasets: ESC-10 (a small research dataset) and FSD50K (a large generalist dataset using the AudioSet ontology).

### File Size Reference:
While I didn't find the exact file size for the STMicroelectronics YAMNet-256 int8 quantized model, I found related YAMNet TFLite models:
- Coral YAMNet classification model: 4.21 MB
- Standard YAMNet TFLite model: 16.1 MB

### Download Locations:
The STMicroelectronics YAMNet-256 models can be found at:
- **Hugging Face**: STMicroelectronics/yamnet repository
- **GitHub**: STMicroelectronics/stm32ai-modelzoo repository under `audio_event_detection/yamnet/ST_pretrainedmodel_public_dataset/`

The model files are typically named `yamnet_256_64x96_tl_int8.tflite` for the int8 quantized versions.

I found comprehensive information about ESP32 mel spectrogram generation, FFT audio preprocessing, and TFLite Micro implementation. Here are the key findings:

## Audio Preprocessing Pipeline

The typical workflow involves: Audio Input (I2S Microphone) → Feature Extraction (MFCC/Mel Spectrogram) → Model Loading (TFLite Micro Model) → Inference Execution → Confidence Output → Action Trigger.

## Mel Spectrogram & FFT Implementation

Raw audio data is processed using mel frequency conversion, FFT and some kind of logarithm. The mel spectrogram generation process includes:

- Mel filter banks map the spectrum to the Mel frequency scale, log transform simulates nonlinear human hearing, and DCT extracts low-dimensional cepstral coefficients (typically 10–13)
- ESP32-S3's DSP instruction set accelerates FFT and DCT operations, achieving 2–3 ms per-frame processing at 16 kHz sampling

## Critical Compatibility Issue

The hardest part is doing feature extraction of audio data in a compatible way for training and inference on the device, making it utterly important to use the same (compatible) implementations for the whole pipeline of Training→Deployment→Usage.

## FFT Processing Details

Fast Fourier transform (FFT) calculates the FFT result which is an array of frequencies using slices of audio data, which is then used to update a spectrogram. The process steps through audio extracting a window of samples on each step and computing the spectrogram, with input samples normalized and copied into the FFT input buffer, and blank areas zeroed out since FFT input is a power of two.

## ESP32 Resources

- The esp-tflite-micro repository provides the component and examples needed to use Tensorflow Lite Micro on Espressif Chipsets using ESP-IDF platform
- KissFFT can be used on ESP32 for creating spectrograms using 16 bit int as input

### Audio Feature Extraction Considerations

For audio feature extraction on ESP32, the raw audio data is typically processed using mel frequency conversion, FFT and some kind of logarithm. ## Key Resources

**Official TFLite Micro Example:**
TensorFlow Lite Micro includes a micro_speech example that demonstrates wake-word recognition using two models: an audio preprocessor that generates spectrogram data from raw audio samples, and a Micro Speech model (less than 20 kB) that can recognize keywords like "yes" and "no".

**Audio Preprocessing:**
The Audio Preprocessor model converts raw audio samples into spectrographic features, with audio samples input in windowed frames that overlap, and when sufficient features accumulate, they're provided to the Micro Speech model.

**ESP32 Implementation:**
Espressif maintains the esp-tflite-micro repository with components and examples for using TensorFlow Lite Micro on ESP32 chipsets (like ESP32-P4) using the ESP-IDF platform.

**Mel Spectrogram Process:**
The audio feature generation pipeline follows: Windowing → FFT → Mel Filters → Log, producing a log-scaled mel filterbank. ESP32-S3's DSP instruction set accelerates FFT and DCT operations, achieving 2–3 ms per-frame processing at 16 kHz sampling.

**Practical Component:**
The ESPMicroSpeechFeatures library is a fork of TensorFlow Lite Micro's Microfrontend that generates spectrogram features from audio samples.

Based on my research, I need to inform you that **YAMNet-1024 is not feasible on ESP32-S3**. However, there's a viable alternative that will work. Let me explain:

## The Problem with YAMNet-1024

[YAMNet-1024](https://huggingface.co/STMicroelectronics/yamnet) has **3.2 million parameters** and the model file is approximately **3.9 MB**. According to [this discussion](https://github.com/tensorflow/models/issues/10241), it's not feasible to run yamnet.tflite on microcontrollers like the ESP32-S3.

Performance data shows that a ~2MB model on ESP32-S3 [takes about 60 seconds for inference](https://github.com/espressif/esp-tflite-micro/issues/94) when using PSRAM, compared to 50ms on PC. Your ESP32-S3 has only ~[225KB of fast SRAM available](https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf/issues/10281) for heap after system overhead.

## The Solution: YAMNet-256

[STMicroelectronics provides YAMNet-256](https://huggingface.co/STMicroelectronics/yamnet/blob/main/README.md), a downsized version specifically optimized for microcontrollers:

**Specifications:**
- Model size: **~135-167 KB** (int8 quantized) - fits in ESP32-S3 SRAM ✅
- Output: **256-dimensional embeddings** (instead of 1024)
- Input: 16kHz mono audio - matches your mic setup ✅  
- Preprocessing: 64-mel, 96-frame spectrograms
- Parameters: 130K (vs 3.2M for YAMNet-1024)

The implementation will require:

The hardest part is mel-spectrogram generation. [TFLite Micro's micro_speech example](https://github.com/tensorflow/tflite-micro/tree/main/tensorflow/lite/micro/examples/micro_speech) includes audio preprocessing that generates spectrograms, and [ESPMicroSpeechFeatures](https://github.com/kahrendt/ESPMicroSpeechFeatures) is a PlatformIO component that provides this functionality.

However, yamnet-256 expects:
- **64 mel filterbanks** (vs micro_speech's 40)
- **96 frames** (0.96 seconds per patch)
- FFT window: 25ms, hop: 10ms
- Frequency range: 125-7500 Hz

**2. TFLite Micro Integration**

[Espressif's esp-tflite-micro](https://github.com/espressif/esp-tflite-micro) provides optimized TensorFlow Lite Micro support for ESP32-S3, with [DSP acceleration achieving 2-3ms per-frame processing](https://zediot.com/blog/esp32-s3-tensorflow-lite-micro/) at 16kHz.

**3. Memory Strategy**

For 3 seconds of audio at 16kHz:
- Raw audio: 48,000 samples × 2 bytes = **96 KB**
- Mel-spectrogram: 64 × 96 × 4 bytes (float) = **24.6 KB**
- Model weights: **~167 KB**
- Tensor arena: **~50-100 KB** (estimated)
- Total: **~340-390 KB** - will need PSRAM for some buffers

   132→    encode(&tokenizer, prompt, 1, 0, prompt_tokens, &num_prompt_tokens);

   137→        return;

   142→    int next;
   143→    int token = prompt_tokens[0];
   144→    int pos = 0;
   145→
   146→    while (pos < steps) {

   148→        v4sf* logits = forward(&transformer, token, pos);
   149→
   150→        // Check for failure

   152→            Serial.println("\nERROR: Forward pass failed (SD streaming issue)");
   153→            free(prompt_tokens);
   154→            return;

   156→

   161→            next = sample(&sampler, logits);
   162→        }
   163→        pos++;
   164→
   165→        // Check for end of sequence
   166→        if (next == 1) break;
   167→
   168→        // Decode and print token

   175→                }
   176→            } else {

   178→            }
   179→        }
   180→
   181→        token = next;
   182→

   184→        if (start_time == 0) {
   185→            start_time = millis();
   186→        }

   188→

    18→void malloc_run_state(RunState* s, Config* p) {
    19→    int kv_dim = (p->dim * p->n_kv_heads) / p->n_heads;
    20→
    21→    // Allocate activation buffers in PSRAM (not heap!)
    22→    s->x = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    23→    s->xb = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    24→    s->xb2 = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    25→    s->hb = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->hidden_dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    26→    s->hb2 = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->hidden_dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    27→    s->q = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    28→    s->key_cache = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->n_layers * p->seq_len * kv_dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    29→    s->value_cache = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->n_layers * p->seq_len * kv_dim, sizeof(v4sf));
    30→    s->att = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->n_heads * p->seq_len, sizeof(v4sf));
    31→    s->logits = (v4sf*)ps_calloc(p->vocab_size, sizeof(v4sf));
    32→
    33→    if (!s->x || !s->xb || !s->xb2 || !s->hb || !s->hb2 || !s->q ||
    34→        !s->key_cache || !s->value_cache || !s->att || !s->logits) {
    35→        Serial.println("ERROR: RunState PSRAM allocation failed!");
    36→    }
    37→}
    38→
    39→void free_run_state(RunState* s) {
    40→    free(s->x);
    41→    free(s->xb);
    42→    free(s->xb2);
    43→    free(s->hb);
    44→    free(s->hb2);
    45→    free(s->q);
    46→    free(s->att);
    47→    free(s->logits);
    48→    free(s->key_cache);
    49→    free(s->value_cache);
    50→}

    56→void calculate_layer_offsets(Transformer* t) {
    57→    // Calculate byte offset for each layer's weights in the model file
    58→    Config* p = &t->config;
    59→    int head_size = p->dim / p->n_heads;
    60→    size_t offset = sizeof(Config); // Start after config header
    61→
    62→    // Token embedding table (shared, loaded to PSRAM)
    63→    offset += p->vocab_size * p->dim * sizeof(v4sf);
    64→
    65→    // For each layer, calculate offsets
    66→    for (int l = 0; l < p->n_layers; l++) {
    67→        t->layer_offsets[l].offset = offset;
    68→        size_t layer_size = 0;
    69→
    70→        // RMS attention weight
    71→        layer_size += p->dim * sizeof(v4sf);
    72→
    73→        // Attention weights (wq, wk, wv, wo)
    74→        layer_size += p->dim * (p->n_heads * head_size) * sizeof(v4sf); // wq
    75→        layer_size += p->dim * (p->n_kv_heads * head_size) * sizeof(v4sf); // wk
    76→        layer_size += p->dim * (p->n_kv_heads * head_size) * sizeof(v4sf); // wv
    77→        layer_size += (p->n_heads * head_size) * p->dim * sizeof(v4sf); // wo
    78→
    79→        // RMS FFN weight
    80→        layer_size += p->dim * sizeof(v4sf);
    81→
    82→        // FFN weights (w1, w2, w3)
    83→        layer_size += p->dim * p->hidden_dim * sizeof(v4sf); // w1
    84→        layer_size += p->hidden_dim * p->dim * sizeof(v4sf); // w2
    85→        layer_size += p->dim * p->hidden_dim * sizeof(v4sf); // w3
    86→
    87→        t->layer_offsets[l].size = layer_size;
    88→        offset += layer_size;
    89→
    90→        Serial.printf("Layer %d: offset=%zu size=%zu KB\n", l,
    91→                      t->layer_offsets[l].offset,
    92→                      t->layer_offsets[l].size / 1024);
    93→    }
    94→}

## TensorFlowLite_ESP32 Library

I found relevant information about the Arduino_TensorFlowLite_ESP32 micro_speech example and its mel/spectrogram preprocessing code:

## Repository and Example

The Arduino_TensorFlowLite_ESP32 library runs TensorFlow machine learning models on microcontrollers and includes a speech recognition sample.(no content)The audio_provider and command_responder must be modified according to the environment in which they are used.

## Spectrogram Preprocessing Details

The TensorFlow Lite model works with spectrograms, which are two dimensional arrays that are made up of slices of frequency information, each taken from a different time window.

**Key preprocessing parameters:**
- Each frequency slice is created by running an FFT across a 30ms section of the audio sample data.
- Input samples are treated as being between -1 and +1 as real values (encoded as -32,768 and 32,767 in 16-bit signed integer samples), resulting in an FFT with 256 entries.
- Every sequence of six entries is averaged together, giving a total of 43 frequency buckets in the final slice.

## Python Example Code

A Python function for generating spectrograms normalizes the audio, creates the spectrogram using window_size=320 and stride=160, reduces frequency bins using average pooling, and applies log10 transformation.

For the actual C++ implementation code, you can find it in the audio_provider.cc file in the micro_speech example within the Arduino_TensorFlowLite_ESP32 GitHub repository.

I found the STMicroelectronics YAMNet models on Hugging Face! Here's what I discovered:

## Main Repository
STMicroelectronics provides YAMNet audio classification models on Hugging Face, including a downsized YAMNet-256 version that outputs embeddings of size 256 for microcontrollers, and the original YAMNet-1024 with 3.2 million parameters for use on the STM32N6.

**Repository URL:** https://huggingface.co/STMicroelectronics/yamnet

## Model Details
- YAMNet-256 is quantized in int8 using TensorFlow Lite converter, and YAMNet-1024 is quantized using ONNX quantizer
- Both models expect mel-spectrogram patches of size 64x96, format (n_mels, n_frames)
- YAMNet-256 is provided for two datasets: ESC-10 and FSD50K, with the FSD50K model trained to detect: Knock, Glass, Gunshots and gunfire, Crying and sobbing, Speech

## Download Location
To download the TFLite models, visit the Hugging Face repository and navigate to the "Files and versions" tab where the model files (.tflite) should be available for download.

**Additional Resource:** The models are also available in the STMicroelectronics STM32 AI Model Zoo on GitHub at: https://github.com/STMicroelectronics/stm32ai-modelzoo

// yamnet_audio_embedding.ino - YAMNet-1024 Audio Embedding on ESP32-S3
// Records 3-5 seconds of audio, extracts 1024-D embeddings, saves to SD card
// Uses dual-core optimization and SD card model streaming

#include <SD.h>
#include <SPI.h>
#include "audio_recorder.h"
#include "mel_spectrogram.h"
#include "yamnet_inference.h"
#include "embedding_writer.h"

// SD card SPI pins (shared with LCD)
#define SD_CS   41
#define SD_MOSI 38
#define SD_MISO 40
#define SD_SCK  39

// Model file on SD card
const char* MODEL_PATH = "/yamnet1024.tflite";
const char* OUTPUT_PATH = "/embedding.json";

// Audio configuration
const int RECORD_SECONDS = 3;  // 3-5 seconds configurable
const int SAMPLE_RATE = 16000;
const int TOTAL_SAMPLES = RECORD_SECONDS * SAMPLE_RATE;

// Global instances
AudioRecorder audio_recorder;
MelSpectrogram mel_processor;
YamNetInference yamnet;
EmbeddingWriter writer;

// Buffers (allocated in PSRAM)
int16_t* audio_buffer = nullptr;
float* mel_features = nullptr;
float* embeddings = nullptr;

bool system_ready = false;

void setup() {
    Serial.begin(115200);
    delay(1000);

    Serial.println("\n========================================");
    Serial.println("YAMNet-1024 Audio Embedding");
    Serial.println("ESP32-S3 Dual-Core Optimized");
    Serial.println("========================================\n");

    // Print memory info
    Serial.printf("Total heap: %d bytes\n", ESP.getHeapSize());
    Serial.printf("Free heap: %d bytes\n", ESP.getFreeHeap());
    Serial.printf("Total PSRAM: %d bytes\n", ESP.getPsramSize());
    Serial.printf("Free PSRAM: %d bytes\n", ESP.getFreePsram());
    Serial.println();

    // Initialize SD card
    Serial.print("Mounting SD card... ");
    SPI.begin(SD_SCK, SD_MISO, SD_MOSI, SD_CS);
    if (!SD.begin(SD_CS)) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK");

    uint64_t cardSize = SD.cardSize() / (1024 * 1024);
    Serial.printf("SD Card Size: %llu MB\n\n", cardSize);

    // Allocate buffers in PSRAM
    Serial.print("Allocating audio buffer... ");
    audio_buffer = (int16_t*)ps_malloc(TOTAL_SAMPLES * sizeof(int16_t));
    if (!audio_buffer) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK");

    Serial.print("Allocating mel-spectrogram buffer... ");
    mel_features = (float*)ps_malloc(MEL_BINS * MEL_FRAMES * sizeof(float));
    if (!mel_features) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK");

    Serial.print("Allocating embeddings buffer... ");
    embeddings = (float*)ps_malloc(EMBEDDING_DIM * sizeof(float));
    if (!embeddings) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK\n");

    // Initialize audio recorder
    Serial.print("Initializing I2S microphone... ");
    if (!audio_recorder.begin(SAMPLE_RATE)) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK");

    // Initialize mel-spectrogram processor
    Serial.print("Initializing mel-spectrogram processor... ");
    if (!mel_processor.begin(SAMPLE_RATE)) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK");

    // Load YAMNet model from SD card
    Serial.println("Loading YAMNet-1024 model from SD...");
    if (!yamnet.begin(MODEL_PATH)) {
        Serial.println("FAILED");
        error_halt();
    }
    Serial.println("OK");

    Serial.printf("\nMemory after initialization:\n");
    Serial.printf("Free heap: %d bytes\n", ESP.getFreeHeap());
    Serial.printf("Free PSRAM: %d bytes\n", ESP.getFreePsram());
    Serial.println();

    system_ready = true;

    Serial.println("========================================");
    Serial.println("READY! System will auto-record on boot");
    Serial.println("========================================\n");
}

void loop() {
    if (!system_ready) {
        delay(1000);
        return;
    }

    // Run once on boot
    Serial.printf("Recording %d seconds of audio...\n", RECORD_SECONDS);
    unsigned long start_time = millis();

    if (!audio_recorder.record(audio_buffer, TOTAL_SAMPLES)) {
        Serial.println("ERROR: Recording failed!");
        error_halt();
    }

    unsigned long record_time = millis() - start_time;
    Serial.printf("Recording complete: %lu ms\n\n", record_time);

    // Generate mel-spectrogram
    Serial.println("Generating mel-spectrogram (64x96)...");
    start_time = millis();

    if (!mel_processor.compute(audio_buffer, TOTAL_SAMPLES, mel_features)) {
        Serial.println("ERROR: Mel-spectrogram failed!");
        error_halt();
    }

    unsigned long mel_time = millis() - start_time;
    Serial.printf("Mel-spectrogram complete: %lu ms\n\n", mel_time);

    // Run YAMNet inference (dual-core optimized)
    Serial.println("Running YAMNet-1024 inference...");
    Serial.println("(Using dual-core optimization)");
    start_time = millis();

    if (!yamnet.infer(mel_features, embeddings)) {
        Serial.println("ERROR: Inference failed!");
        error_halt();
    }

    unsigned long infer_time = millis() - start_time;
    Serial.printf("Inference complete: %lu ms\n\n", infer_time);

    // Print first few embedding values
    Serial.println("Embeddings (first 10 values):");
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        Serial.printf("  [%d]: %.6f\n", i, embeddings[i]);
    }
    Serial.println();

    // Save to SD card as JSON
    Serial.printf("Writing embeddings to %s...\n", OUTPUT_PATH);
    start_time = millis();

    if (!writer.writeJSON(OUTPUT_PATH, embeddings, EMBEDDING_DIM)) {
        Serial.println("ERROR: Write failed!");
        error_halt();
    }

    unsigned long write_time = millis() - start_time;
    Serial.printf("Write complete: %lu ms\n\n", write_time);

    // Print performance summary
    Serial.println("========================================");
    Serial.println("PERFORMANCE SUMMARY");
    Serial.println("========================================");
    Serial.printf("Recording:       %lu ms\n", record_time);
    Serial.printf("Mel-spectrogram: %lu ms\n", mel_time);
    Serial.printf("YAMNet inference: %lu ms\n", infer_time);
    Serial.printf("JSON write:      %lu ms\n", write_time);
    Serial.printf("TOTAL:           %lu ms\n", record_time + mel_time + infer_time + write_time);
    Serial.println("========================================\n");

    Serial.println("SUCCESS! Embeddings saved to SD card.");
    Serial.println("System halting (power cycle to run again).\n");

    // Halt - run once per boot
    while(1) {
        delay(1000);
    }
}

void error_halt() {
    Serial.println("\nSYSTEM HALTED DUE TO ERROR");
    Serial.println("Check wiring and SD card contents");
    while(1) {
        delay(1000);
    }
}

// audio_recorder.cpp - I2S audio recording implementation

#include "audio_recorder.h"

AudioRecorder::AudioRecorder() : initialized_(false), sample_rate_(16000) {
}

AudioRecorder::~AudioRecorder() {
    end();
}

bool AudioRecorder::begin(int sample_rate) {
    sample_rate_ = sample_rate;

    // I2S configuration for INMP441 microphones
    i2s_config_t i2s_config = {
        .mode = (i2s_mode_t)(I2S_MODE_MASTER | I2S_MODE_RX),
        .sample_rate = sample_rate_,
        .bits_per_sample = I2S_BITS_PER_SAMPLE_32BIT,
        .channel_format = I2S_CHANNEL_FMT_RIGHT_LEFT,  // Stereo
        .communication_format = I2S_COMM_FORMAT_STAND_I2S,
        .intr_alloc_flags = ESP_INTR_FLAG_LEVEL1,
        .dma_buf_count = 4,
        .dma_buf_len = 1024,
        .use_apll = false,
        .tx_desc_auto_clear = false,
        .fixed_mclk = 0
    };

    i2s_pin_config_t pin_config = {
        .bck_io_num = MIC_BCK_PIN,
        .ws_io_num = MIC_WS_PIN,
        .data_out_num = I2S_PIN_NO_CHANGE,
        .data_in_num = MIC_DIN_PIN
    };

    // Install and configure I2S driver
    if (i2s_driver_install(I2S_PORT, &i2s_config, 0, NULL) != ESP_OK) {
        return false;
    }

    if (i2s_set_pin(I2S_PORT, &pin_config) != ESP_OK) {
        i2s_driver_uninstall(I2S_PORT);
        return false;
    }

    initialized_ = true;
    return true;
}

bool AudioRecorder::record(int16_t* buffer, int num_samples) {
    if (!initialized_) {
        return false;
    }

    int samples_written = 0;

    // Read from I2S and downmix stereo to mono
    while (samples_written < num_samples) {
        size_t bytes_read = 0;

        if (i2s_read(I2S_PORT, i2s_buffer_,
                     I2S_BUFFER_SIZE * sizeof(int32_t),
                     &bytes_read, portMAX_DELAY) != ESP_OK) {
            return false;
        }

        int samples_read = bytes_read / sizeof(int32_t);

        // Convert and downmix: stereo (L,R,L,R...) -> mono
        for (int i = 0; i < samples_read && samples_written < num_samples; i += 2) {
            // Extract left and right channels (32-bit to 16-bit)
            int16_t left = (int16_t)(i2s_buffer_[i] >> 16);
            int16_t right = (int16_t)(i2s_buffer_[i + 1] >> 16);

            // Simple average downmix to mono
            buffer[samples_written++] = ((int32_t)left + (int32_t)right) / 2;
        }
    }

    return true;
}

void AudioRecorder::end() {
    if (initialized_) {
        i2s_driver_uninstall(I2S_PORT);
        initialized_ = false;
    }
}

// mel_spectrogram.h - Mel-spectrogram generation for YAMNet
// Generates 64 mel bins × 96 frames from 16kHz audio
// Uses ESP-DSP for accelerated FFT

#ifndef MEL_SPECTROGRAM_H
#define MEL_SPECTROGRAM_H

#include <Arduino.h>

// YAMNet input requirements
#define MEL_BINS 64          // Number of mel filterbanks
#define MEL_FRAMES 96        // Number of time frames
#define FFT_SIZE 512         // FFT window size (25ms @ 16kHz)
#define HOP_LENGTH 160       // Hop size (10ms @ 16kHz)
#define SAMPLE_RATE 16000    // Audio sample rate

class MelSpectrogram {
public:
    MelSpectrogram();
    ~MelSpectrogram();

    // Initialize with sample rate
    bool begin(int sample_rate);

    // Compute mel-spectrogram from audio samples
    // Output: mel_features[MEL_BINS * MEL_FRAMES] in row-major order
    bool compute(int16_t* audio, int num_samples, float* mel_features);

    // Cleanup
    void end();

private:
    // Initialize mel filterbank
    void initMelFilterbank();

    // Apply mel filterbank to power spectrum
    void applyMelFilterbank(float* power_spectrum, float* mel_output);

    // Compute single FFT frame
    void computeFFTFrame(int16_t* audio, int start_idx, float* power_spectrum);

    // Convert frequency to mel scale
    float hzToMel(float hz);
    float melToHz(float mel);

    int sample_rate_;
    bool initialized_;

    // Mel filterbank (MEL_BINS × (FFT_SIZE/2 + 1))
    float* mel_filterbank_;

    // Working buffers
    float* fft_input_;
    float* fft_output_;
    float* window_;
};

#endif // MEL_SPECTROGRAM_H
